narrative:
The model estimated a 59.8% chance that you would fail the bar exam on the first attempt. That is above a coin flip, so your application was denied because the review treated bar-exam risk as too high, not because failure is certain.

The strongest factor was your third-year class standing. Your third-year decile was 1, far below the average of about 5.8 among accepted students, and this was the largest push toward a failure prediction. Your LSAT score of 38 was slightly above the accepted-student average of about 37.2; this was the second most influential factor, but it pushed in the opposite direction, toward passing. Your upper-middle family-income background was the third most influential factor and also slightly favored passing; it is common among accepted students, so it did not drive the rejection.

To improve your position, ask for a file review or holistic reconsideration and provide context for your third-year performance. Focus first on strengthening your academic record, such as additional advanced coursework or a clear explanation of any disruption. Consider retaking the LSAT only if practice tests show a meaningful gain. Applying to programs that review applications holistically and seeking pre-law advising can help you present a stronger case next time.
